title: The Weekend the Dollar Let Go of Gold
short_title: The Dollar Lets Go of Gold
subtitle: Camp David, the 'Nixon shock' and the Smithsonian Agreement, 1971
intro: For twenty-five years the money of the Western world had rested on one promise. Other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and foreign central banks could hand in their dollars at the US Treasury for gold at $35 an ounce. By the summer of 1971 there were far more dollars abroad than gold in Fort Knox, Germany had already let the mark float, and on 12 August over a billion dollars more was pushed onto European central banks.

On Friday 13 August, Richard Nixon took about fifteen advisers to Camp David and told them to make no outside calls. The State Department and the National Security Council were not told. On Sunday night he went on television and announced that the dollar would no longer be converted into gold, alongside a wage-price freeze and a 10 percent import surcharge. From then on the dollar was backed by nothing but the willingness of people to keep using it.

The record of the weekend is mostly American and official: the address in the Public Papers, the State Department's Foreign Relations volume, and H. R. Haldeman's diary, which he dictated each night and which the Nixon Library has transcribed. Arthur Burns's private diary, published in 2010, gives the dissent. William Safire, Paul Volcker, Charles Coombs and Herbert Stein wrote years later and are labelled so. Abroad, most voices come through US memoranda that recorded them, through Satō Eisaku's diary in Tokyo, and through a Japanese economist's note dated three days after the yen began to float.

Some gaps remain. Nothing by Lord Cromer was found on the British request that American memoirs call the final straw, and British papers deny it was ever a request for gold. Pierre-Paul Schweitzer of the IMF appears only through an American memo. Japanese finance officials, Giscard d'Estaing in Paris and the press of Le Monde and Asahi left records that this chapter could not consult directly.

Was it necessary? At the time Connally argued that the shock would force surplus countries to revalue, and Shultz, close to Milton Friedman, preferred floating rates in any case. Volcker's later account treats a run on the remaining gold as only days away. Against that, Burns warned of a run on the dollar, retaliation abroad and blame falling on the President, and Europeans and Japanese protested a decision taken without them. Later critics link the end of the gold anchor to the inflation of the 1970s, while defenders say the fixed system could not have survived. The records here show each side's reasoning rather than settle the question.

The repair came on 18 December 1971 at the Smithsonian Institution, where new parities were set and the dollar was devalued against gold, though it stayed unconvertible. Nixon called it the most significant monetary agreement in the history of the world. It lasted fourteen months: after a second devaluation in February 1973, the major currencies were floating by March 1973.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Tokyo is thirteen hours ahead of Washington in summer: Nixon's address at 9 p.m. EDT on Sunday 15 August was heard in Japan at 10 a.m. on Monday 16 August, after the Tokyo exchange market had opened. That is why Japanese records date the shock to 16 August. Cable times in FRUS are in GMT ('Z').
seam: A promise of gold had stood behind the world's money since 1944. Over one weekend, a few people in a lodge with the phones barred turned it into a promise of nothing but continued use, and the money went on working. Burns feared the change would break the system, the markets held, and from then on the dollar's value rested on agreement alone. As in The City & the City, everyone kept living in the same economy while agreeing not to look closely at what now held it up, and the people outside the room, in London, Bonn and Tokyo, were told after the decision was made.

eyes.name: Richard Milhous Nixon
eyes.role: Aged 58; 37th President of the United States
eyes.where: Camp David, Maryland, 13–15 August; the White House for the broadcast; the Smithsonian Institution in December
eyes.form: official record (televised address, remarks, diplomatic message)
eyes.authenticity: The address and the Smithsonian remarks are printed in the Public Papers of the Presidents: Richard M. Nixon, 1971 (the address at pp. 886–891) and reproduced by the American Presidency Project. His message to Chancellor Brandt is FRUS 1969–1976 vol. III, doc. 169. These are public statements and official cables, not private writing; his own later memoir is not used here.
eyes.bio: Nixon took the decision in a closed weekend meeting and announced it as part of a domestic package, with the wage-price freeze given first place. The records show a president presenting the end of gold convertibility as a defence of the dollar against speculators rather than as a forced retreat. Four months later he hailed the settlement that patched the system as historic.

sources.title: Address to the Nation Outlining a New Economic Policy: 'The Challenge of Peace' (American Presidency Project)
Remarks Announcing a Monetary Agreement Following a Meeting of the Group of Ten, 18 Dec 1971
FRUS 1969–1976 vol. III, doc. 169 (message to Brandt)

eyes.name: Harry Robbins (H. R.) Haldeman
eyes.role: Aged 45; White House Chief of Staff
eyes.where: The White House and Camp David
eyes.vantage_label: in the room, keeping the nightly record
eyes.authenticity: Haldeman dictated his diary most nights; the tapes and transcripts are part of the Nixon presidential materials and are posted by the Richard Nixon Presidential Library. A selection was published as The Haldeman Diaries (1994), pp. 340–346 covering this weekend. Digests here rest on the Library transcripts and the Library's almanac summaries.
eyes.bio: Haldeman sat in on the Camp David sessions and dictated what he had heard the same night. His diary is the nearest thing to a running log of the weekend: who argued for what, how secrecy was kept, and how the President wanted credit shared out afterwards. He wrote as a political manager, so the record is strong on staging and reaction and thin on monetary theory.

sources.title: Haldeman diary transcript, 13 Aug 1971 (Nixon Library)
Haldeman diary transcript, 15 Aug 1971 (Nixon Library)
Nixon Library almanac, 12 Aug 1971
Nixon Library almanac, 16 Aug 1971

eyes.name: Arthur Frank Burns
eyes.role: Aged 67; Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
eyes.authenticity: Burns kept a private diary from 1969 to 1974. It was published as Inside the Nixon Administration: The Secret Diary of Arthur Burns, 1969–1974, ed. Robert H. Ferrell (University Press of Kansas, 2010). Modern publication: digests only; the entries are known here through quotation in secondary articles, not a reading of the book.
eyes.bio: Burns was the one senior figure at Camp David who argued against closing the gold window, warning of a run on the dollar and retaliation abroad. His diary records both his resistance and his acceptance once the decision went the other way. It also records an uneasy, sometimes contemptuous relationship with the President he served.

sources.title: Mises Institute, 'Burns Diary Exposes Myth of Fed Independence' (review with diary excerpts)
BullionStar, British requests for $3 billion (quotes the 12 Aug entry)

eyes.name: John Bowden Connally Jr.
eyes.role: Aged 54; Secretary of the Treasury, former Democratic governor of Texas
eyes.where: Texas, then Washington and Camp David; Rome in November
eyes.form: recorded by others; official record; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: Connally left no diary for these days. His views are known from Haldeman's diary, Treasury and State records in FRUS vol. III, and later accounts by colleagues (Coombs 1976, Volcker 1992). His own memoir, In History's Shadow (1993), is a later firsthand account not consulted here.
eyes.bio: Connally, a politician rather than a financier, pressed hardest for closing the window and using the shock to force other countries to revalue. Nixon wanted him credited as the 'quarterback' of the plan. In the autumn he carried the hard line into negotiations with the Group of Ten.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168 (Camp David editorial note)
FRUS vol. III, doc. 210 (Rome, November 1971)

eyes.name: Paul Adolph Volcker Jr.
eyes.role: Aged 43; Under Secretary of the Treasury for Monetary Affairs
eyes.where: Washington; Camp David; London on 16 August; Rome in November
eyes.vantage_label: the technician who carried the news abroad
eyes.authenticity: His actions are documented in FRUS vol. III (docs. 169, 170, 210), US government records. His own account is Changing Fortunes: The World's Money and the Threat to American Leadership (1992), written with Toyoo Gyohten of Japan's Ministry of Finance: later firsthand, modern copyright, summarised only.
eyes.bio: Volcker had worked on contingency plans for suspending convertibility and briefed the weekend on gold losses. Within hours of the broadcast he was explaining it to the diplomatic corps, and the next afternoon to European and Japanese officials in London. His later book, co-written with a Japanese finance official, is one of the few accounts that sets the American and Japanese sides together.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 170 (London meeting, 16 Aug 1971)
FRUS vol. III, doc. 169

eyes.name: William Lewis Safire
eyes.authenticity: Before the Fall: An Inside View of the Pre-Watergate White House (1975) draws on Safire's notes from the time; FRUS cites it (p. 511) for the list of those present. Later firsthand; modern copyright, summarised only.
eyes.bio: Safire was the only professional writer at Camp David and was given the job of shaping the speech. His later book is the source for who was actually there, from a guest book he kept. He brings the view of a man whose job was to turn a technical retreat into a story the country would accept.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168 (cites Before the Fall, p. 511)

eyes.name: Herbert Stein
eyes.role: Aged 55; member of the Council of Economic Advisers
eyes.authenticity: His recollections used here come from an interview given to the FRUS editor on 8 April 1998 and quoted in FRUS vol. III, doc. 168: a later firsthand account recorded in a US government publication. His book Presidential Economics (1984) gives a further later account.
eyes.bio: Stein, a professional economist, later admitted that the people in the room did not all know what they had decided. His testimony is the plainest statement that the weekend was improvised as well as secret.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168

eyes.name: Robert David Hormats
eyes.role: Aged 28; economist on the National Security Council staff
eyes.where: The White House (outside the Camp David meeting)
eyes.vantage_label: foreign-policy staff left out of the room
eyes.authenticity: His memoranda to Henry Kissinger of 13 and 21 August 1971 are printed in FRUS vol. III (doc. 167 and the editorial note doc. 172). US government records, quotable.
eyes.bio: Hormats wrote for Kissinger, whose National Security Council was not represented at Camp David and did not know the meeting had begun. His 13 August memo describes the crisis as it looked from outside the room on the very afternoon the decision was being taken. A week later he was relaying the IMF's ideas for repairing the damage.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 167
FRUS vol. III, doc. 172

eyes.name: Charles A. Coombs
eyes.role: Aged 53; Senior Vice President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, in charge of foreign exchange operations
eyes.vantage_label: the central banker who handled the request
eyes.authenticity: The Arena of International Finance (1976): later firsthand, modern copyright. Known here through quotation in a secondary article and Barry Popik's phrase research; summarised only.
eyes.bio: Coombs ran the New York Fed's dealings with foreign central banks and is the witness closest to the British request. His later account directly contradicts the version that became Washington folklore. He is also the earliest printed source for Connally's most quoted remark.

sources.title: BullionStar, British requests for $3 billion (quotes Coombs)
Barry Popik, 'It's our currency, but it's your problem'

eyes.name: Rowland Baring, 3rd Earl of Cromer
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. British Ambassador in Washington, former Governor of the Bank of England; known here only through American memoirs and British official papers about the episode
eyes.vantage_label: the request that may have tipped it
eyes.form: official record (British government papers); recorded by others
eyes.authenticity: No diary or letter by Cromer on the request was found. The British side survives in Bank of England file OV53/60 (10 Aug memo) and the Prime Minister's file PREM 15/838 (13 Aug HM Treasury letter), as quoted in a secondary article. Whether Britain asked for gold, for a guarantee, or for $3 billion or $750 million is contested.
eyes.bio: Several American accounts say the British ambassador came to the Treasury around 12 August asking for 'cover' on some $3 billion of British dollar holdings. British papers deny any request for gold and reject the $3 billion figure. He stands here as a gap in the record: the man at the centre of the most repeated story of the week left no account of it that was found.

sources.title: BullionStar, British requests for $3 billion (quotes OV53/60 and PREM 15/838)

eyes.name: Otmar Emminger
eyes.role: Aged 60; Vice-President of the Deutsche Bundesbank
eyes.vantage_label: European central banker at the table
eyes.form: recorded by others (US memorandum of conversation)
eyes.authenticity: His words of 16 August are known from the US memorandum of conversation (FRUS vol. III, doc. 170), drafted 23 August by S. Y. Cross: an official record of what he said, not his own text. His memoir D-Mark, Dollar, Währungskrisen (1986) is a later firsthand account not consulted here.
eyes.bio: Emminger had lived through the May 1971 inflows that forced Germany to close its exchange market and float the mark. In London he spoke for the country most exposed to the dollar's weakness. His insistence that every currency's position be credible states the problem the Smithsonian talks would try to solve.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 170

eyes.name: Pierre-Paul Schweitzer
eyes.role: Aged 59; Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund
eyes.authenticity: His public statements of August 1971 were not located for this chapter; his proposals are known here through Robert Hormats's memo of 21 August 1971 as summarised in FRUS vol. III, doc. 172. Secondhand.
eyes.bio: The IMF was the referee of the Bretton Woods system, and the United States had not consulted it. Schweitzer answered with a single plan to rebuild what had broken. Washington's coolness towards his ideas, and his later departure from the Fund in 1973, show how far the decision had been taken out of the institution's hands.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III, doc. 172

eyes.name: Satō Eisaku
eyes.authenticity: Satō Eisaku nikki, published in six volumes by Asahi Shimbunsha (1997–99). Modern publication: digest only. The December entries used here are known through their paraphrase in a nippon.com article, not a reading of the diary itself.
eyes.bio: Satō had already been surprised in July by Nixon's announcement of a visit to China; the dollar measures were the second 'Nixon shock' in a month. He leaned heavily on his finance ministry, which kept the Tokyo market open and spent heavily to hold the old rate. His diary records a leader uncertain what the new rate would do to his country.

sources.title: nippon.com, 'The Nixon Shock of 1971 and Today's "Cheap Japan"' (Japanese edition)
Ando, Japan's Foreign Economic Policy and Relations with the United States (National Security Archive)

eyes.name: Asada Shirō (麻田四郎)
eyes.role: Japanese economist writing in Shōgaku tōkyū (商学討究), the economics journal of Otaru University of Commerce
eyes.authenticity: 'ニクソン・ショックについての覚え書' (A memorandum on the Nixon shock), Shōgaku tōkyū vol. 22 nos. 2–3, pp. 19–28, dated 31 August 1971; digitised in the Otaru University of Commerce repository. Modern copyright: digest only.
eyes.bio: Asada dated his note within three days of Japan letting the yen float. It is a record of how the weeks looked from a Japanese university: a list of shocks, statements and market confusion before anyone knew where the yen would settle.

sources.title: Asada, 'ニクソン・ショックについての覚え書' (Otaru repository PDF)

entries.headline: A Quadriad meeting leaves Burns alarmed at the President
entries.digest: Months before the crisis, Burns records a meeting of the President's top economic advisers at which Nixon struck him as agitated and close to irrational. The entry shows the strain between the Fed chairman and the White House well before Camp David. It is the background to Burns's later sense that his advice on gold would not carry the day.
entries.source_note: Burns diary, ed. Ferrell (2010), as excerpted in the Mises Institute review; date as given there.

entries.headline: Pieces of the package had been studied for months
entries.digest: Stein later told the FRUS editor that parts of the August programme had been examined earlier in 1971 at the Council of Economic Advisers, the Budget office and the Treasury. No full options paper reached Camp David, but the ideas were not new. The plan was improvised in assembly, not in conception.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168, citing the editor's interview with Herbert Stein, 8 April 1998; months not specified.

entries.headline: A Bank of England memo weighs demanding American gold
entries.digest: A Top Secret Bank of England memo lists, among Britain's options as the dollar weakened, a demand for a massive amount of gold from the Americans. It adds that the Americans would probably refuse and close the gold window. The memo records an option considered, not a request made.
entries.source_note: Bank of England file OV53/60, 10 Aug 1971, as quoted in BullionStar (Manly). The archive file itself was not consulted.

entries.headline: Connally calls from Texas and the President decides
entries.digest: Haldeman records Connally phoning from Texas with news of bad days on the gold market and a warning that things were getting worse abroad. Connally saw the President at 5:30 that afternoon, and afterwards Nixon decided to go ahead with the plan. The key economic officials, Burns included, were to be gathered at Camp David that weekend. That evening the Nixons went to a performance at Wolf Trap.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary, 12 Aug 1971, as summarised on the Nixon Library almanac page for that date; tape 273-20 (5:30–7:00 p.m.) logs the meeting.

entries.headline: Burns senses his fight for the gold window is lost
entries.digest: In his diary Burns writes that his efforts to stop the closing of the gold window appear to have failed. He does not name Britain or any other trigger. The entry shows that the decision was effectively made before the Camp David weekend began.
entries.source_note: Burns diary, 12 Aug 1971, as quoted in BullionStar (Manly); wording known only at second hand.

entries.headline: The British ask for cover on their dollars
entries.digest: In his later account Volcker dates to this Thursday a British request for unspecified devaluation cover on about $3 billion of their dollar holdings. He writes that if Britain, the dollar's closest partner, was going to take gold for its dollars, the old game was over. His book treats the request as the final straw rather than the cause.
entries.source_note: Volcker and Gyohten, Changing Fortunes (1992), as quoted in BullionStar (Manly); other accounts date the request 11 or 13 August.

entries.headline: The ambassador's visit that became Washington legend
entries.digest: Several American memoirs and histories say Lord Cromer came to the Treasury around this date asking for some $3 billion of 'cover', usually described as gold. A file title in the Prime Minister's papers speaks of a Bank of England demand for conversion of $750 million into gold. No account by Cromer himself was found, and the size and nature of the request remain disputed.
entries.source_note: Volcker (1992), Coombs (1976), Graetz, Nichter and others as compiled by BullionStar; PREM 15/838 file title as quoted there.

entries.place: Federal Reserve Bank of New York / Washington
entries.headline: Coombs calls the $3 billion story a travesty
entries.digest: Coombs later recalled Connally announcing that the British had come in to ask the United States to cover $3 billion. Coombs, who handled such operations, called that version a travesty of the facts. In his telling the request was smaller and was quickly agreed at $750 million.
entries.source_note: Coombs, The Arena of International Finance (1976), as quoted in BullionStar; Nichter (2015) has the request received by Coombs on 13 August.

entries.headline: London denies asking for gold
entries.digest: A letter from the Chancellor of the Exchequer's office to Downing Street states that the Bank of England never asked for conversion of dollars into gold and that there was no basis for a figure of $3 billion. The wording covers the Bank of England, not the Treasury-run Exchange Equalisation Account that held Britain's reserves, so it does not settle the question.
entries.source_note: PREM 15/838, 13 Aug 1971, as quoted in BullionStar (Manly). Original not consulted.

entries.headline: From outside the room: an erosion of confidence
entries.digest: On the afternoon the Camp David meeting began, Hormats briefed Kissinger on a crisis whose meeting he did not know about. He traced the trouble to a year-long erosion of European confidence in the dollar, the German float in May, and over $1 billion pushed onto European central banks on 12 August alone. He thought a European revaluation the likeliest way out.
entries.quote: Throughout 1971 there has been an erosion of European confidence in the stability of the dollar.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 167 (Hormats to Kissinger, 13 Aug 1971; Confidential). US government record.

entries.headline: Helicopters, separate flights and no outside calls
entries.digest: Haldeman notes that the President left for Camp David about 2:30 p.m. and that others flew up separately so their movements would not be noticed. The meeting in the Aspen lounge ran from 3:15 to 7:00 p.m. Nixon ordered that no one make outside calls and that everything stay secret until the announcement.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary transcript, 13 Aug 1971, Nixon Library (tape AC-12 A/B); times match FRUS doc. 168.

entries.headline: Connally for closing, Burns against
entries.digest: Haldeman records Volcker briefing on gold losses and general agreement that something had to be done. Connally wanted to close the gold window and let the dollar float; Burns opposed, warning of political risk, a run on the dollar and retaliation abroad, and that the President would be blamed. Volcker had doubts about pairing an import tax with the closing. Nixon wanted Connally fully on board.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary transcript, 13 Aug 1971 (Nixon Library); FRUS doc. 168 likewise notes Burns's unsuccessful attempt to keep the window open.

entries.headline: A short speech, and an argument over the day
entries.digest: The President wanted a short address, about ten minutes and some 1,500 words, with Safire as editor and Haldeman to brief the media and business. Haldeman records Burns pressing for a Sunday announcement and the President inclined to Monday. In the end he spoke on Sunday night, before markets opened.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary transcript, 13 Aug 1971 (Nixon Library), read in summary; the Monday/Sunday detail is as the transcript was summarised and should be checked against the printed Haldeman Diaries, pp. 340–346.

entries.headline: The guest book: who was there
entries.digest: Safire's later book lists those at Camp David from a guest book, adding names the President's diary omits: Caspar Weinberger and Arnold Weber of the budget office, Kenneth Dam, Treasury's Michael Bradfield and Haldeman's aide Larry Higby. Nobody from the State Department or the National Security Council is on either list. Fewer than twenty people knew.
entries.source_note: Safire, Before the Fall (1975), p. 511, as cited in FRUS vol. III, doc. 168.

entries.headline: No one was sure whether this meant a float
entries.digest: Stein later said it was not clear to the people in the room whether closing the gold window implied letting the dollar float. There was little discussion of what the decision meant for relations with allies. The State Department and NSC were not represented.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168, quoting the editor's interview with Stein, 8 April 1998.

entries.headline: Burns argues, loses, and accepts
entries.digest: Burns's diary covers the Camp David meeting itself. He favoured keeping the gold window open but accepted the decision to close it once it was taken. Reviewers note that he regarded the closing as temporary; it became permanent.
entries.source_note: Burns diary, ed. Ferrell (2010), as described in the Mises Institute review; exact entry dates not given there.

entries.headline: Drafting 'The Challenge of Peace'
entries.digest: Safire spent the weekend turning the decisions into a broadcast. The text put the freeze on wages and prices and the jobs measures first, the gold suspension later, and cast the move as a strike against speculators. Haldeman's diary confirms he was the editor; the later memoir is his own account of the work.
entries.source_note: Safire, Before the Fall (1975); role confirmed by Haldeman, 13 Aug. Day of drafting approximate.

entries.headline: Tell the Secretary of State
entries.digest: On the Saturday the President said Secretary of State Rogers should be informed, and asked whether he would accept a 10 percent cut in foreign aid. The State Department was learning of a major foreign-policy decision after it had been made.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 168, citing Haldeman's notes for 14 Aug.

entries.headline: The speculators' war and the suspension of convertibility
entries.digest: Nixon told the country that speculators had been waging war on the dollar and that he had directed Connally to stop converting dollars into gold. The decisive words were placed well into a speech about jobs and prices. Foreign governments were not consulted.
entries.quote: In recent weeks, the speculators have been waging an all-out war on the American dollar. ... suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets
entries.source_note: Public Papers of the Presidents: Richard Nixon, 1971, pp. 886–891; American Presidency Project text.

entries.headline: Freeze, surcharge, and a promise about the dollar
entries.digest: The same address ordered a 90-day freeze on wages and prices and a temporary 10 percent tax on imports. Nixon assured Americans that the step would not cost them at home. The measures for the world were sold as protection for the household.
entries.quote: your dollar will be worth just as much tomorrow as it is today.
entries.source_note: Public Papers 1971, pp. 886–891; American Presidency Project text.

entries.headline: 'Very strongly positive': the first reaction
entries.digest: Haldeman records that the President, calling him right after the broadcast, felt good about it and had wanted an emotional lift in it. No advance text was released and no TelePrompTer used. Nixon wanted Connally credited as quarterback to his own coach, and Burns built up and sent to talk to the financial writers. The first reaction, Haldeman notes, was strongly positive.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary transcript, 15 Aug 1971 (Nixon Library, tape AC-12B).

entries.headline: Briefing the diplomats, then the night flight
entries.digest: That night Volcker briefed the Washington diplomatic corps on the new measures, and the State Department sent a summary to posts abroad. He then flew to London to meet European and Japanese officials the next day.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 169 and its source note (circular telegram 149446; full transcript sent 25 Aug as telegram 156086).

entries.headline: A personal message to Brandt
entries.digest: Identical messages went to other heads of government that evening. To Willy Brandt, Nixon listed the measures and said he knew they would worry Germany. He asked for early talks on the monetary and trading system and said Connally would consult the German finance minister.
entries.quote: I recognize that these actions will be of concern to Germany as they are vital to us. ... It was our responsibility to act and we have done so.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 169 (State to Embassy Bonn, 16 Aug 1971, 0245Z).

entries.headline: A Cabinet briefing and a record day on Wall Street
entries.digest: Haldeman records a Cabinet meeting on the freeze and the import surcharge, and the record stock market gain. The President played golf with Secretary Rogers at Burning Tree and a meeting with congressional leaders was set for the next day. The New York Fed later recorded the Dow up a record 32.93 points that day.
entries.source_note: Haldeman diary, 16 Aug 1971, as summarised on the Nixon Library almanac page; Dow figure from the NY Fed Monthly Review, Sept 1971, p. 204ff.

entries.headline: No return to gold, and no deal on rates
entries.digest: Volcker told French, German, Italian, Japanese and British officials that the United States had not come to negotiate exchange rates and would not return to a gold-based system. He said the surcharge would end once the American payments position was strong. He suggested an informal ministers' meeting in Washington on 21–22 August.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 170 (drafted 23 Aug by S. Y. Cross, approved by Volcker).

entries.headline: Markets cannot stay shut for long
entries.digest: Emminger said German markets could not remain closed for more than about three days and that both the dollar and other currencies needed credible positions. Germany's state secretary Schöllhorn doubted any country would willingly revalue. The Europeans feared reopening at the old rates and a long period of floating.
entries.quote: The dollar position must be credible and the position of other currencies must be credible.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 170 (US record of the London meeting).

entries.headline: Daily reports on foreign reaction begin
entries.digest: From this day the State Department sent Kissinger daily memoranda on foreign reactions. Press coverage abroad was harsh, while governments concentrated on adapting. Most anger was directed at the 10 percent surcharge rather than the gold suspension. Most exchange markets stayed closed all week.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 172.

entries.headline: The IMF's plan, and a warning on protectionism
entries.digest: Hormats reported that Schweitzer had proposed a single package covering exchange rates, the surcharge, wider margins, the gold price and restored convertibility. He agreed with the Treasury that a large meeting would get nowhere, but urged the United States to say what it wanted and warned that protectionism abroad could escalate.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 172, summarising Hormats's memo of 21 Aug 1971.

entries.headline: The Fund proposes to rebuild the whole system
entries.digest: As relayed by the NSC staff, Schweitzer put forward an integrated plan rather than piecemeal fixes: new rates, the surcharge's removal, wider bands, a change in the gold price and a return to convertibility. The proposal shows the IMF trying to restore the old order the United States had just stepped out of.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 172 (Hormats memo, 21 Aug 1971). Schweitzer's own statements not consulted; date is that of the memo.

entries.headline: 360 yen ends
entries.digest: Asada records the yen's move to a floating rate on 28 August. For two weeks Tokyo had stayed open while the finance ministry and Bank of Japan bought some $3.9 billion to defend the old rate of 360. His note is written in the first days of the float.
entries.source_note: Asada note (dated 31 Aug 1971) for the float date; the $3.9 billion figure is from Jiji Press, not Asada.

entries.headline: A Japanese economist lists the shocks
entries.digest: Asada sets out the chain of events as seen from Japan: the eight-point yen package of 6 June, Nixon's China announcement of 15 July, reports on 12 August of an American proposal for wider bands, then the 'dollar defence' package. He notes the government and Bank of Japan statements upholding the parity and the confusion in the exchange market. He writes after the yen began to float on 28 August.
entries.source_note: Asada, 'ニクソン・ショックについての覚え書', Shōgaku tōkyū 22 (2–3), dated 31 Aug 1971 (Otaru repository).

entries.headline: The American package goes to the Deputies
entries.digest: At the Group of Ten deputies' meeting Volcker set out the American proposal and argued it had to be taken as a whole. Nine delegations said publishing it before the ministers met would make Washington less flexible; the French objected to a passage on dual exchange markets.
entries.quote: The position had to be seen as a package.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 210.

entries.headline: Connally tells the Italians to stop hiding behind institutions
entries.digest: Before the ministerial meeting, Connally heard Italy's Treasury minister say the American paper had worried all the Europeans. He replied that Washington had always named three issues: realignment, trade and the sharing of defence burdens. He urged that the heads of government could decide where officials could not.
entries.quote: we cannot afford to be bogged down by hide-bound institutional arrangements
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, doc. 210.

entries.headline: 'Our currency, but your problem'
entries.digest: The most quoted line of the crisis, that the dollar was America's currency but other countries' problem, first appears in print attributed to Connally in Coombs's 1976 book. Coombs does not say when or where it was said. Later writers place it at the Rome meetings, without a contemporary report.
entries.source_note: Coombs (1976), p. 219, per Barry Popik's research; the Rome setting is a later attribution.

entries.headline: 'The most significant monetary agreement'
entries.digest: After two days of Group of Ten talks, Nixon came to the Smithsonian to announce new rates. The United States would ask Congress to devalue the dollar against gold and would drop the import surcharge. The dollar stayed unconvertible.
entries.quote: the most significant monetary agreement in the history of the world
entries.source_note: Public Papers 1971; American Presidency Project, 'Remarks Announcing a Monetary Agreement Following a Meeting of the Group of Ten'.

entries.headline: Revaluation will bring a recession
entries.digest: After the yen was fixed at 308 to the dollar, a rise of 16.88 percent and the largest of any currency, Satō wrote that the revaluation would probably cause a recession and hoped it would not be severe.
entries.source_note: Satō Eisaku nikki, paraphrased in nippon.com (Japanese); exact entry date not given there.

entries.headline: The market rises, and he cannot read it
entries.digest: The next day the Tokyo stock market went up. Satō wrote that he found it hard to judge what was happening. A prime minister who had promised to defend 360 yen was now living with 308.
entries.source_note: Satō Eisaku nikki, paraphrased in nippon.com; the promise to keep 360 is reported in Ando (National Security Archive).

convergences.label: Thursday: the decision before the weekend
convergences.note: Haldeman records Nixon deciding after seeing Connally; Burns writes that his fight seems lost; Volcker, twenty years later, dates the British request to the same day; and the British papers deny it. Four records of one day disagree about what tipped it.

convergences.label: Friday: Camp David opens in secret
convergences.note: Inside, Haldeman logs the argument and Safire the guest list; Stein later admits no one was sure what the decision meant. Outside, Hormats briefs Kissinger on a crisis without knowing the meeting exists, while London and the New York Fed are writing contradictory versions of the British request.

convergences.label: Sunday night: the broadcast
convergences.note: Nixon speaks of a war waged by speculators; Haldeman records the President's relief and his plans for sharing credit; Volcker briefs the diplomats and leaves for London. The public speech, the private diary and the diplomatic cable give three versions of the same evening.

convergences.label: Monday: markets answer
convergences.note: Wall Street posts a record gain while Tokyo, the one major market left open, sees heavy dollar selling and European exchanges stay shut. In London Volcker refuses gold and Emminger warns that the German market cannot stay closed for long. Nixon's cable to Brandt has arrived overnight.

convergences.label: The IMF tries to rebuild
convergences.note: Schweitzer's integrated plan reaches the White House only through an NSC memo, and the Treasury is cool. The Fund that was meant to run the system is consulted after the decision, not before.

convergences.label: Japan lets the yen go
convergences.note: After two weeks of buying dollars, Tokyo floats the yen. Asada, writing three days later, records a list of shocks and statements; Satō, who had leaned on his finance ministry to hold 360, would by December be writing of recession.

convergences.label: Rome: the Group of Ten
convergences.note: The official record shows Volcker insisting on a package and Connally impatient with institutions. Coombs's memoir supplies the remark later attached to Rome, which the record of the meetings does not contain.

convergences.label: The Smithsonian settlement
convergences.note: In Washington Nixon calls it the most significant monetary agreement in history; in Tokyo Satō writes of recession and cannot read the market. The yen's 16.88 percent rise was the largest of the realignment.

ties.note: Haldeman was Nixon's chief of staff and dictated his record of the weekend each night, including what Nixon told him by phone after the broadcast.
At Camp David Connally argued for closing the gold window and Burns against; Haldeman's diary records the clash.
Nixon overruled Burns, then asked that he be 'built up' and sent to brief the financial press. Burns's diary records his growing dismay at the President.
Volcker was Connally's under secretary; Connally set the political line and Volcker carried it to London and Rome.
They sat across the table in London on 16 August 1971, recorded in the same US memorandum of conversation.
Both were inside the American financial establishment, yet their later memoirs give different sizes and meanings to the British request.
Coombs's memoir is a main source for the British request associated with Cromer, whose own account was not found.
Hormats's memo of 21 August is the record through which Schweitzer's plan appears here.
Safire drafted the speech Nixon gave on 15 August.
Both were at Camp David, and both gave later accounts: Safire in a 1975 memoir, Stein in a 1998 interview.
Haldeman's diary is the same-day record of Burns's warnings that he would later echo in his own diary.
Both of the year's 'Nixon shocks', the July China announcement and the August dollar measures, reached Satō's government without prior consultation.
Two Japanese records of the same months, one from a provincial economist's desk, one from the Prime Minister's diary.

threads_out.note: The Rentenmark of 1923 had no gold behind it, only a mortgage, a limit on issue and public confidence. In 1971 the dollar's last link to gold was cut, and confidence became its only backing as well.

Closing the gold window cancelled, by one country's decision, a promise to foreign central banks that they could redeem their dollars in gold. Like the debt proclamations of older states, it rewrote obligations from above, and those who held the claims bore the change.
The fixed-rate system that broke in 1971 was designed at Bretton Woods in July 1944, while the war in Europe was still being fought, around a dollar convertible into gold at $35 an ounce.

Connally's demands in Rome included 'burden sharing' for American defence costs. US forces stationed in West Germany, reinforced during the Berlin crisis, were part of the dollar outflow that built up in European central banks.
